headline: Websites are blocking AI agents from accessing services, raising questions about their future usefulness.
summary: Major websites like Yelp, Delta, and Amazon are preventing AI agents from performing tasks due to security concerns and the impact on ad revenue, challenging the utility of autonomous AI.
details: AI agents from OpenAI, Meta, and Google aim to automate online tasks from booking reservations to shopping. However, popular web services are actively preventing these agents from operating.
Companies like Yelp, Delta Air Lines, JPMorgan Chase, and Charles Schwab are blocking AI agents. Reasons cited include data licensing requirements and security concerns over account access.

Amazon has been in a legal battle with AI startup Perplexity over its agentic shopping feature. Amazon argues third-party agents should respect service provider decisions, while Perplexity likens agents to user extensions.
Despite these challenges, Meta has partnered with retailers such as Walmart, Gap, and Sephora to allow its Muse agent to shop on their sites. Shopify has also opened its network to AI agents.
Experts note that widespread blocking significantly impacts the perceived value of AI agents. If agents cannot access many online services, their utility for users is greatly diminished.
caption:
AI agents promised to do everything for you online, but major websites are actively blocking them. What does this mean for the future of autonomous AI?

AI agents from OpenAI, Meta, and Google aim to automate online tasks from booking reservations to shopping. However, popular web services are actively preventing these agents from operating.

Companies like Yelp, Delta Air Lines, JPMorgan Chase, and Charles Schwab are blocking AI agents. Reasons cited include data licensing requirements and security concerns over account access.

Amazon has been in a legal battle with AI startup Perplexity over its agentic shopping feature. Amazon argues third-party agents should respect service provider decisions, while Perplexity likens agents to user extensions.

Despite these challenges, Meta has partnered with retailers such as Walmart, Gap, and Sephora to allow its Muse agent to shop on their sites. Shopify has also opened its network to AI agents.

Experts note that widespread blocking significantly impacts the perceived value of AI agents. If agents cannot access many online services, their utility for users is greatly diminished.

headline: Taiwan targets illicit AI server exports to China with five-year prison terms
summary: New export controls align Taiwan with US trade bans, making smuggling AI servers and chips a criminal offense punishable by up to five years in prison and a $92,500 fine.
details: Taiwan is expanding its list of controlled exports to include AI servers and the latest chips, aligning its policies with the U.S.'s trade bans. After these export controls take effect, anyone caught smuggling these items will face criminal charges.

Violators will be prosecuted under the Foreign Trade Act, which carries a severe penalty of up to five years in prison and/or a fine of around $92,500. This move is a significant step in curbing the illicit flow of advanced technology.

Taiwan's Minister of Economic Affairs stated that future measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones, following commitments made in a reciprocal trade agreement signed earlier this year. The U.S. has actively sought to prevent the smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips into China.

Previously, Taiwan did not treat AI chip exports to China as a crime, requiring charges under other laws. This new expansion of the Foreign Trade Act will simplify prosecution, similar to how Singapore charged suspected Nvidia AI GPU smugglers with fraud and money laundering.

This will be one of the strictest measures by the Taiwanese government against exports to China, a move that will likely be welcomed by Washington. However, it is also expected to provoke Beijing, which has previously condemned Taipei's export restrictions on companies like Huawei and SMIC.
